title: Management of Patients on Mechanical Ventilation
path: Management of Patients on Mechanical Ventilation

headings.title: Introduction to Mechanical Ventilation and Indications
headings.content: Mechanical ventilation is a life-saving supportive therapy used in critical care nursing to assist or replace spontaneous breathing when a patient's respiratory system is compromised. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding the foundational concepts and clear clinical indications for mechanical ventilation is crucial for managing acute respiratory distress in hospital settings. Indications for mechanical ventilation generally fall into two broad categories: acute respiratory failure (either hypoxemic, hypercapnic, or a combination of both) and the need to protect the airway. Hypoxemic respiratory failure often arises from conditions like severe pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), or pulmonary edema, where the lungs cannot adequately oxygenate the blood despite supplemental oxygen. Hypercapnic respiratory failure occurs when there is inadequate alveolar ventilation to eliminate carbon dioxide, commonly seen in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, neuromuscular diseases such as Myasthenia Gravis, or central nervous system depression caused by drug overdoses or traumatic brain injuries. Additionally, patients who are hemodynamically unstable, have severe facial trauma, or are unable to maintain their own airway due to a diminished level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale typically 8 or less) require mechanical ventilation to secure the airway and reduce the work of breathing. Nurses play a pivotal role in identifying early signs of respiratory fatigue, such as tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, paradoxical breathing, and altered mental status, ensuring timely intervention and initiation of ventilatory support before full respiratory arrest occurs.

headings.title: Types of Mechanical Ventilators and Modes
headings.content: Mechanical ventilators are sophisticated medical devices designed to deliver a controlled flow of gas to a patient's lungs. Understanding ventilator classification and modes is essential for safe nursing practice in intensive care units. Ventilators are broadly categorized into negative-pressure ventilators (such as the historical 'iron lung') and positive-pressure ventilators, which are predominantly used in modern clinical practice. Positive-pressure ventilators push air into the lungs during inspiration, overcoming airway resistance and lung compliance. Ventilator modes dictate how the machine interacts with the patient's spontaneous breathing efforts. Common modes include Controlled Mandatory Ventilation (CMV), where the ventilator delivers breaths at a set rate and volume regardless of patient effort, primarily used for heavily sedated or paralyzed patients. Assist-Control (AC) ventilation allows the patient to trigger a breath, but the ventilator delivers a pre-set volume or pressure for every breath initiated, ensuring a minimum minute ventilation. Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV) delivers a set number of mandatory breaths synchronized with the patient's inspiratory effort while allowing the patient to breathe spontaneously between mandatory breaths without machine assistance. Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) is a spontaneously triggered mode where the ventilator provides a boost of pressure during inspiration to overcome the resistance of the artificial airway. Understanding these modes helps nursing students monitor patient-ventilator synchrony, recognize dyssynchrony, and anticipate physician orders based on the patient's recovery trajectory.

headings.title: Initial Setup, Settings, and Baseline Assessment
headings.content: The initial setup and baseline assessment of a patient newly placed on a mechanical ventilator establish the standard for ongoing critical care monitoring. Once an artificial airway—such as an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube—is successfully placed and confirmed, the multidisciplinary team connects the patient to the ventilator with prescribed initial settings. Typical initial settings include fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2), tidal volume (usually based on ideal body weight, approximately 6 to 8 mL/kg), respiratory rate, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and inspiratory flow rate. Immediately following setup, nurses must perform a comprehensive baseline assessment to ensure correct tube placement and patient stabilization. This involves auscultating bilateral breath sounds to rule out mainstem bronchial intubation (typically the right mainstem), observing symmetrical chest expansion, and checking carbon dioxide levels via colorimetric end-tidal CO2 detectors or continuous capnography. The nurse must also verify that the endotracheal tube is securely anchored at the correct lip or gum line and document the centimeter marking. Baseline hemodynamic parameters—including heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation via pulse oximetry, and arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis—must be evaluated within 15 to 30 minutes of initiation to assess the effectiveness of oxygenation and ventilation, allowing for prompt adjustments by the healthcare team.

headings.title: Routine Nursing Care and Patient Monitoring
headings.content: Routine nursing care and vigilant patient monitoring are essential to prevent complications and promote recovery in mechanically ventilated patients. The critical care nurse must perform systematic head-to-toe assessments at least every two to four hours. Respiratory monitoring includes observing chest wall movement, checking ventilator parameters (such as peak inspiratory pressure and exhaled tidal volume), and continuously monitoring pulse oximetry and capnography. High peak pressures can indicate airway obstruction, bronchospasm, biting on the tube, or decreased lung compliance, prompting immediate nursing investigation. Cardiovascular stability must also be closely monitored, as positive-pressure ventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, which can reduce venous return and cardiac output, leading to hypotension. Nurses must frequently assess sedation levels using validated tools like the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) to prevent patient distress and accidental extubation while avoiding over-sedation. Nutritional support, typically via enteral feeding tubes, must be managed carefully with regular checks of gastric residual volumes and elevation of the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees, unless contraindicated. Furthermore, comprehensive skin care, passive and active range of motion exercises, and regular eye care are vital nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries, contractures, and corneal abrasions in immobile, critically ill patients.

headings.title: Airway Management and Endotracheal Suctioning
headings.content: Airway management and endotracheal suctioning are core psychomotor skills for nurses caring for mechanically ventilated patients. Artificial bypass of the upper airway impairs the normal mechanisms of humidification, filtration, and warming, leading to thick, viscous secretions that can obstruct the airway. Therefore, adequate humidification of inspired gases is mandatory. Endotracheal suctioning is performed to remove accumulated pulmonary secretions and maintain a patent airway, but it must be executed strictly based on clinical need—such as visible secretions in the tube, coarse crackles over the trachea, sawtooth patterns on the flow-volume loop, or sudden drops in oxygen saturation—rather than on a routine schedule. Prior to suctioning, the nurse should pre-oxygenate the patient with 100% oxygen for a brief period to prevent suction-induced hypoxemia. Sterile technique is paramount, whether using open suction systems or closed (in-line) suction systems, to prevent the introduction of pathogens into the lower respiratory tract. The suction catheter should be inserted gently without applying suction until it reaches the desired depth (usually just beyond the tip of the endotracheal tube), followed by intermittent suctioning and rotation of the catheter during withdrawal. Suctioning passes should not exceed 10 to 15 seconds to minimize hypoxia, mucosal trauma, and cardiac dysrhythmias caused by vagal stimulation.

headings.title: Prevention of Ventilator-Associated Complications
headings.content: Mechanically ventilated patients are vulnerable to numerous secondary complications that significantly impact morbidity, mortality, and length of stay in the intensive care unit. Preventing these complications is a primary responsibility of the nursing team. Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) is one of the most serious nosocomial infections; it can be significantly reduced by adhering to the 'VAP bundle,' which includes maintaining head-of-bed elevation at 30 to 45 degrees, daily interruption of sedation with readiness-to-wean assessments, oral care with chlorhexidine gluconate at least every 2 to 4 hours, and subglottic secretion drainage when available. Barotrauma and volutrauma are mechanical complications caused by high airway pressures and excessive tidal volumes, leading to alveolar rupture, pneumothorax, or subcutaneous emphysema; nurses must monitor for sudden decreases in breath sounds, tracheal deviation, and high-pressure ventilator alarms. Oxygen toxicity can result from prolonged exposure to high FiO2 levels, causing cellular damage and absorption atelectasis. Stress-induced gastrointestinal ulcers (Curling's ulcers) are mitigated through prophylactic proton pump inhibitors or H2 receptor antagonists. Additionally, deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis using sequential compression devices (SCDs) and low-molecular-weight heparin is critical due to prolonged immobility. Finally, intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICUAW) is addressed through early mobilization protocols and physical therapy consultation as soon as the patient is hemodynamically stable.

headings.title: Ventilator Weaning and Extubation Protocols
headings.content: Ventilator weaning and extubation protocols represent the transition from mechanical support back to spontaneous, unassisted breathing. Weaning should begin as soon as the underlying condition that necessitated mechanical ventilation has improved and the patient meets specific clinical criteria. Nurses actively participate in daily spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs) to evaluate the patient's readiness for liberation from the ventilator. Criteria for initiating a weaning trial include adequate oxygen saturation (e.g., SpO2 > 90% on FiO2 <= 0.4 or PEEP <= 5 cmH2O), hemodynamic stability without significant vasopressor support, adequate spontaneous tidal volume, reversal of the acute phase of the underlying illness, and the ability to initiate spontaneous respiratory efforts. During an SBT—often conducted using T-piece trials or low levels of pressure support (e.g., PS 5-8 cmH2O with PEEP 5)—nurses closely monitor the patient for signs of respiratory fatigue or distress, such as tachypnea (respiratory rate > 35 breaths/min), tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, agitation, or a drop in oxygen saturation. If the patient tolerates the SBT successfully for 30 to 120 minutes, the interprofessional team evaluates them for extubation. Extubation involves suctioning the endotracheal tube and oropharynx, deflating the cuff, and smoothly removing the tube during peak inspiration or expiration while encouraging the patient to cough. Post-extubation care requires close monitoring for upper airway edema, stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory insufficiency, ensuring emergency re-intubation equipment is readily available.

headings.title: Patient and Family Support in Critical Care
headings.content: Patient and family support in critical care is a vital aspect of holistic nursing, particularly when a patient is tethered to a mechanical ventilator. The intensive care environment can be profoundly frightening, disorienting, and overwhelming for both the patient and their loved ones. Because artificial airways prevent verbal communication, mechanically ventilated patients often experience severe anxiety, frustration, and helplessness. Nurses must implement alternative communication strategies, such as providing communication boards, alphabet boards, writing pads, or utilizing simple hand gestures and lip-reading techniques. Regular reassurance, orientation to time and place, and explaining every nursing procedure before performing it help reduce patient fear. Family members experience high levels of stress, fear of loss, and helplessness when seeing their relative surrounded by complex machinery. Nursing support for families involves clear, compassionate, and jargon-free explanations of the ventilator's purpose, daily progress updates, encouraging flexible visitation policies when clinically appropriate, and integrating family members into simple care activities. Providing emotional support, facilitating spiritual care if requested, and connecting families with social work or counseling services are essential nursing interventions that promote psychological well-being and coping during critical illness.
